decisions.reason: Ehrenberg (1977) empirically re-tests the church-attendance equations and household time-allocation model from his own prior published paper, Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975) ('specified as similarly as possible to those estimated in our previous paper', explicitly identified in footnote 3 as Azzi and Ehrenberg 1975, tables 5 and 6). Shipped erroneously named Long and Settle (1977), which is a concurrent replication of Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975) published in the same journal issue that Ehrenberg critiques in footnote 1 as one of 'the two new contributions' rather than re-testing.

decisions.reason: For the tested original study (Azzi and Ehrenberg, 1975), the direct replication of the church-attendance equations in Section I explicitly yields 'mixed support': female mean attendance exceeds male mean attendance in 8 of 9 denominations, the predicted age-attendance profile holds in 16 of 18 cases, and control variables perform similarly to the previous paper, but in contrast the female age-attendance profile is steeper than the male profile in only 4 of 9 cases, education increases attendance, and family income has no systematic effect. Section II (1969 National Jewish Population Study) supports the life-cycle and relative-wage implications while noting lower mean female than male synagogue attendance as a 'contradiction' in footnote 9, and the conclusion notes that 'the evidence is not totally unambiguous' while supporting the usefulness of the general household time-allocation framework. Both shipped and blind coded 'mixed', with blind properly evaluating the outcome against Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975).

initial_expert_decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent (never previously adjudicated). In this 1977 Journal of Political Economy paper ('Household Allocation of Time and Religiosity: Replication and Extension'), Ehrenberg uses new survey data from the 1965 National Fertility Survey (over 5,600 females and their spouses, Tables 1 and 2) and the 1969 National Jewish Population Study (2,427 families, Table 3) to re-estimate annual church/synagogue attendance equations specified as similarly as possible to Tables 5 and 6 of Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975, 'Household Allocation of Time and Church Attendance', J.P.E. 83, no. 1: 27-56, explicitly cited in the opening paragraph, footnote 3, and the reference list), finding mixed support in the fertility survey and strong support in the Jewish population survey. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 2254, Long & Settle, 1977, 'Household Allocation of Time and Church Attendance: Some Additional Evidence', J.P.E. 85, no. 2: 409-413, doi:10.1086/260572) is a separate replication paper by different authors published in the same 1977 JPE issue that also tested Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975); Ehrenberg critiques Long and Settle's methodology in footnote 1 to motivate his own replications, but does not re-analyze Long and Settle's data or re-estimate their specific models. Report equivalence does not apply because Long and Settle (1977) and Azzi and Ehrenberg (1975) are distinct works by different author teams.
